title: Gaps Between Peaks and Dips in a Chain
statement:
You get the head of a singly linked list. A node is a turning point if it has a node on both sides and its value is either strictly greater than both neighbours (a peak) or strictly smaller than both (a dip). The first and last nodes are never turning points.

Number the nodes 0, 1, 2, … from the head. Return [closest, farthest]: the smallest and the largest distance in positions between two different turning points. If there are fewer than two turning points, return [-1, -1].

examples.why: 1 is a dip (position 1), 3 a peak (2), 2 a dip (3). Neighbouring ones are 1 apart; the outer two are 2 apart.
The two 5s are equal, so neither is strictly greater than both neighbours. There are no turning points.
Only the 6 (position 1) and the 7 (position 5) qualify. The flat run of 2s has no strict dip.

hints: To decide whether a node is a turning point you only need its previous value and its next value. Can you walk with that window?
The farthest pair is always the first turning point and the last one. The closest pair is always two turning points that are next to each other in order.
Walk once, remembering the position of the first turning point and of the most recent one. Each new one updates the closest gap; at the end, last − first is the farthest.

explain.intuition:
Turning points come in increasing position order as you walk the list. The largest distance between any two of them must be between the very first and the very last. The smallest distance must be between two that are consecutive in this order: any pair with another turning point in between is longer than the pairs it contains.

So there is no need to compare all pairs, or even to store them. Walk the list with a three-node window (previous value, current node, next node), and keep just two positions: the first turning point and the latest one.
steps: Start with prevVal = head.val, cur = head.next, position i = 1, first = last = -1, closest = ∞.
While cur.next exists, check whether cur.val is strictly above or strictly below both prevVal and cur.next.val.
If it is: when last ≠ -1, update closest with i − last; if first = -1, set first = i. Then set last = i.
If first = last (zero or one turning point) return [-1, -1]; otherwise return [closest, last − first].
pitfalls: Using ≥ or ≤ instead of strict comparisons, which turns plateaus like [2, 5, 5, 1] into peaks.
Counting the head or tail as turning points.
Returning [0, 0] or a real gap when only one turning point exists. One point has no pair, so the answer is [-1, -1].

solutions.title: Collect positions, compare all pairs
solutions.idea: Copy the values to an array, list every turning point's position, and check every pair of positions.

solutions.title: One pass, first and last positions
solutions.idea: The closest pair is always consecutive, and the farthest is first-to-last. Walk once and remember only those positions.

followups: Return the distance between the closest peak and dip only, ignoring peak-to-peak and dip-to-dip pairs.
Treat a flat top like 1, 5, 5, 1 as one peak. How do you change the window?
